The degree of interdependency between two modules

written.q: Explain cohesion and coupling and why a good design has high cohesion and low coupling. Use the kitchen analogy.
written.a: Cohesion: how strongly the parts of a module belong together; coupling: the interdependency between modules. High cohesion makes modules do one specific function; low coupling makes changes local and modules independent. Analogy: the chef does all cooking tasks (high cohesion) and hands plates through a small well-defined opening to the dishwashing station without knowing how it works (low coupling).

written.q: Distinguish software architecture, software design and architectural vs design patterns.
written.a: Architecture is a plan with enough detail to produce a design; design is a plan with enough detail to implement. An architectural pattern is a blueprint used in the designing phase and is the base everything adheres to; a design pattern is an implementation approach in the building phase, structuring classes to solve common problems.

written.q: Compare a developer, tech lead and software architect and list six responsibilities of an architect.
written.a: Developer: implements features, sprint horizon, function/class design. Tech lead: team execution and code quality, sprint/release, task breakdown and standards. Architect: system structure and long-term integrity, months to years, boundaries/tech stack/integration. Architect responsibilities: system decomposition, trade-off analysis, stakeholder communication, quality attribute ownership, decision documentation, technical roadmap.

written.q: Explain ATAM with an example scenario.
written.a: The Architecture Trade-off Analysis Method evaluates a design on paper: identify scenarios (e.g. 10x traffic spike during a sale), map them to quality attributes (scalability, performance), analyse how the current architecture responds, and surface risks and trade-offs (where it breaks and the cost to fix).

written.q: State the five SOLID principles with a violation example for any two.
written.a: SRP: one reason to change. OCP: open for extension, closed for modification. LSP: subclasses replaceable for parents. ISP: no forced dependence on unused methods. DIP: depend on abstractions. Violations: a class that both logs users in and sends emails (SRP); a Penguin subclass of Bird whose fly() throws an error (LSP); an if-else chain edited for each new payment method (OCP).
